Economy · Finance · Opening today

Japan opened a five-day window for capital.

Japan Weeks 2026 begins today. Behind the receptions is a harder question: can Tokyo turn policy language about investment, talent and transition into a market foreigners can actually enter?

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 26, 2026 at 13:30 JST · 6 min read

At 9:00 this morning, an Irish investment-funds seminar opened one of Japan’s busiest finance calendars of the year. By evening, Tokyo’s program would include climate-risk models, disaster finance, asset-management talent, private markets and a reception for industry leaders.

This is Japan Weeks 2026, the fourth edition of a government-backed effort that began in 2023. The official “core week” runs from October 26 to 30, although affiliated events sit on either side. The Financial Services Agency describes the goal directly: promote Japan as a leading asset-management center and strengthen communication with overseas investors.

4thJapan Weeks since the program began in 2023
5 daysofficial core week, October 26–30
30senior ASEAN finance delegates in one study visit

The surprise is how little of the program is about trading screens. Monday’s calendar links capital to physical climate risk, natural-disaster resilience, industrial decarbonization, corporate governance and the recruitment of younger professionals. Japan is not only selling assets. It is selling an institutional story about what money should do.

The week’s real product is access: access to regulators, companies, investors and policy language. Yet many marquee sessions are invitation-only, exposing the central tension between declaring Japan open and making the doorway usable.

From slogan to a room full of specialists

The phrase “asset management nation” can sound abstract. Monday’s schedule translates it into rooms. The Investment Management Association of Japan hosts its fifth industry conference; CFA Society Japan brings students and young professionals into a talent discussion; BNP Paribas convenes a sustainable-future forum; and Polymer Capital and PAG discuss Japan’s macroeconomy and equities.

A separate Mizuho seminar asks how finance can support resilience against increasingly severe disasters through instruments such as resilience bonds and municipal bonds. The timing is unusually concrete: heavy rain is affecting western and eastern Japan on the same day. The weather is not an agenda metaphor; it is the risk the financial models are meant to price.

The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and the GX Acceleration Agency also hold the GGX Finance Summit at Tokyo Prince Hotel and online. Its agenda joins industrial decarbonization with international rulemaking and economic growth. “GX” means green transformation, the Japanese policy shorthand for shifting energy and industry while mobilizing public and private investment.

Why Southeast Asia is inside Japan’s pitch

Japan Weeks is not confined to investors examining Japanese stocks. A five-day GFANZ study visit brings about 30 senior representatives from South and Southeast Asian regulators, central banks, development-finance institutions, commercial banks and institutional investors. Around ten participants come from GFANZ’s Japan chapter.

The program’s stated problem is implementation: transition plans exist, but capital must reach clean energy, infrastructure and industrial projects at scale. Japan’s banks, trading houses and manufacturers have long relationships across Asia, giving Tokyo a possible role between regional projects and global pools of capital.

That role is contested. “Transition finance” can fund real emissions reductions in industries that cannot decarbonize overnight, but weak definitions can also prolong high-carbon assets. The official program itself acknowledges model uncertainty and incomplete disclosure. Investors need to ask which emissions are measured, what timetable is binding and who bears the risk when a technology or policy fails.

What overseas investors are being asked to believe

The government’s pitch rests on several changes: stronger corporate governance, a larger professional asset-management sector, household savings moving toward investment, and easier entry for overseas firms. Japan’s deep capital markets and large pool of household financial assets are the scale behind the message.

But a week of conferences cannot prove that change. Foreign managers will judge licensing, taxation, English-language administration, talent, data quality and the treatment of minority shareholders. Companies will be judged on capital allocation, disclosure and whether boards challenge entrenched practice rather than merely filling formal requirements.

The Financial Services Agency’s official schedule makes the test visible because it puts policy makers and practitioners on the same calendar. A seminar on the revised corporate-governance code can explain intent. Investors will still compare the explanation with votes, buybacks, cross-shareholdings and business exits.

A public week with private doors

Many events are restricted to clients or invited guests. That is normal for financial conferences, where commercially sensitive conversations matter, but it limits how directly the public can evaluate the week. Some sessions are hybrid or provide registration links; others list contacts without a public stream.

The official website remains valuable because it exposes the breadth and ownership of each event. Readers can see which ministry, bank, association or investor organized a session, whether it is online, and what problem it claims to address. That transparency is more useful than treating “Japan Weeks” as one government conference.

By Friday, attention turns to energy security in a multipolar world, linking Japan’s finance pitch to geopolitics. The week therefore moves from climate models and talent pipelines toward the harder constraints of fuel, infrastructure and strategic dependence.

What to measure after the receptions

The meaningful outcomes will not be the number of name cards exchanged. Watch for new fund launches, overseas manager registrations, governance changes, transition-finance standards, cross-border projects and hiring commitments. Those can be checked later against announcements and regulatory data.

Japan Weeks began as a communication vehicle. Its fourth edition shows a more complex claim: Tokyo wants to be a place where global capital can understand Japanese companies, finance Asian transition and find professional talent. This week can open the window. The months after it will show whether anyone can climb through.
